summary: POC scoping call to agree success criteria, workload and benchmark design for an open-model POC to parse and summarize avionics manuals across English, French, and Japanese. Discussed model shortlist (Llama variants, Mistral-like, open instruction-tuned options), tradeoffs between latency/cost/quality, and private vs hosted deployment due to regulatory constraints. Agreed next steps for data share, benchmark template, pricing and kickoff week.
topics: Deployment: Hosted vs Private (VPC/on-prem) and security)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Start time (UTC): 14:00
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Liu (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Redwood SE), Anna Ruiz (AeroNav), Samir Patel (AeroNav), Claire Dubois (AeroNav), Kenji Sato (AeroNav)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): POC to validate extraction and summarization from avionics maintenance manuals, prioritized by safety-critical sections; emphasis on high precision for instructions, multi-lang support, and traceable outputs for audits.

[00:00] Ethan (AE): OK everyone hi, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through the POC scope for the manuals project. quick intro round, then success criteria.
[00:18] Anna (Head of ML): Hi, Anna here. We have Samir, Claire and Kenji with me. we run NLP for tech docs, and this is high priority for Q1 compliance work.
[00:28] Samir (Lead NLP): hey all, we currently have a basic rule-based parser and are testing a transformer fine-tune but throughput and cost are a problem.
[00:36] Maya (SE): great context, thanks. Ethan and I will outline a 4-6 week POC: data collection, benchmarking, integration tests, and a small pilot.
[00:48] Kenji (Localization): want to call out languages: en, fr, ja. we need consistent extraction across all three, especially measured on the Japanese manuals which have different layout patterns.
[01:02] Jordan (SE): quick Q: regulatory requirements — Claire, you mentioned traceability for audits? what does that look like?
[01:10] Claire (Regulatory PM): yes we need per-output provenance: which text segments influenced the summary, stable IDs for paragraphs, and stored audit logs. also data residency — some manuals cannot leave EU/JP.
[01:28] Ethan (AE): good to note — that's why we'll show both hosted and private deployment options. hosted for speed, private (VPC or on-prem) for residency and KMS/HSM integration.
[01:40] Anna: timeline? ideally we want a working integration and benchmark results in 6 weeks. is that realistic?
[01:48] Maya: 6 weeks is tight but doable if data is shared quickly and we scope the eval to a representative subset — say 3k pages sampled across product lines and languages.
[02:02] Samir: on throughput, we expect peak of 12 concurrent users with batch ingestion of ~2k pages nightly; online latency target for API calls is <750ms 95th pct for single-page summaries.
[02:18] Ethan: noted. for capacity planning we will estimate token/s and GPU hours — we'll propose dedicated reserved capacity if they want steady throughput.
[02:30] Anna: success criteria — we have three pillars: accuracy (extract critical instructions with >92% exact-match on our gold labels), hallucination rate below 1% on safety-critical sections, and latency/throughput within cost envelope.
[02:48] Maya: we'll map those to measurable metrics. for accuracy we'll use a combination of token-level exact match and a semantic F1 for paraphrase acceptance. hallucination we'll define as assertions not grounded in source text.
[03:00] Jordan: for bench runner, we usually provide a spreadsheet plus a runner script (python) that reports EM, F1, BLEU for translation checks, and a custom hallucination score. Maya will share.
[03:12] Samir: model shortlist — what are you proposing for open-model options? we prefer open-source for export and on-prem ability.
[03:20] Maya: we're recommending a small shortlist to test tradeoffs: 1) Llama 3.5 instruction-tuned variant (quantized), 2) Mistral-style 8B instruction-tuned open variant, 3) An instruction-following 13B open model (non-Redwood custom) — basically test small-to-medium families to find cost-quality sweet spot.
[03:44] Kenji: do any of these handle Japanese well off-the-shelf? that's the main concern.
[03:50] Maya: Japanese support differs; we expect the 13B variant to have better multilingual pretraining if it's a polyglot model. we'll also include a triage test: tokenization coverage, hallucination per language, and ROUGE/BLEU where applicable.
[04:06] Anna: and domain adaptation? we can't fine-tune large models right away because of cost and ops, so we're planning to try retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and instruction prompts with a small adapter if needed.
[04:18] Ethan: yes RAG + dense retrieval over the manuals and a small adapter or LoRA for safety-critical sections is a common pattern. we'll scope that into the POC as an optional sprint.
[04:30] Samir: what about quantization? we need to know if 4-bit quant gives acceptable quality for our use case.
[04:36] Maya: we'll include quantized runs (4-bit/8-bit) to measure delta in EM and hallucination. historically some precision-sensitive extraction tasks drop ~2-5% with aggressive quant, we'll measure.
transcript_continued:
[05:00] Claire: security — we require SOC2 or equivalent, SSO (SAML), RBAC, and audit logs. plus the residency notes earlier.
[05:12] Ethan: Redwood has SOC2 Type II, SAML/SSO, RBAC, and we can enable private control plane and customer-managed KMS for on-prem. I'll attach the security pack.
[05:24] Anna: cost — we're sensitive. want to avoid multi-million yearly invoices. can we see per-token estimates and a run-rate for the nightly batch?
[05:34] Jordan: we'll create a cost model: token rate per page average (~3k tokens/page), nightly ingestion, and the online per-call cost. also show dedicated reserved capacity numbers vs hosted.
[05:46] Samir: that token estimate seems high — our pages are denser, maybe 1.6k tokens on average. we'll upload sample and you can re-run size calc.
[05:56] Maya: perfect, once you upload sample dataset we'll run an initial token distribution, latency profile, and suggest batching/caching params (prefix cache for repeated boilerplate sections).
[06:08] Ethan: on evaluation, accept thresholds: EM >92% for S1 (safety-critical), hallucination <1%, and average latency 95th <750ms for single page summaries. If model hits those we consider POC success and move to a 3-month pilot.
[06:24] Anna: is there an SLA during POC? we need reliability for the integration tests.
[06:28] Ethan: during POC we offer best-effort for hosted, and for Dedicated we can provide an SLA for uptime/latency if you commit reserved capacity.
[06:36] Kenji: curious about fallback policies: if the main model is overloaded, can the platform route to a smaller cheaper model to avoid outages?
[06:42] Maya: yes we have smart routing and fallback to a compatible model variant; we can configure fallbacks by latency or cost policy. we'll demo that in the pilot.
[06:54] Samir: benchmarks — what runner scripts and metrics will you provide?
[06:58] Maya: EM, token-F1, custom hallucination detector, latency histograms, and per-language breakdowns. Also suggestion: add a 'criticality-weighted' score so safety sections count more.
[07:12] Anna: good, please prioritize the safety-weighted metrics.
[07:18] Ethan: deployment options: 1) hosted Redwood API (fastest), 2) Dedicated reserved GPU pool in our cloud region (predictable throughput), 3) Private deployment (VPC or on-prem) for the strictest residency/KMS requirements. we will outline pros/cons in the POC doc.
[07:36] Claire: for private, can we run in our EU data center and keep keys in our HSM?
[07:40] Jordan: yes that's supported, but it will require extra setup time — estimate 2-3 weeks to provision and connect.
[07:48] Samir: integration: we want a small API shim to map our paragraph IDs into the prompt and return provenance pointers. how does Redwood preserve paragraph IDs through generation?
[07:58] Maya: we recommend including paragraph ids as special tokens in the context and using KV caching to preserve alignment. misc note: transcription may show KV as "K V" sometimes, sorry for the auto-transcribe.
[08:10] Ethan: any blockers on your side?
[08:12] Anna: data privacy approvals — Claire will need to sign off on the sample share. Also need procurement timeline for a pilot budget.
[08:20] Claire: procurement expects a SOW and cost estimate, ideally before 2027-11-12.
[08:26] Ethan: we'll aim to get that to you.
[08:30] Kenji: language testing — can you include tokenization coverage and char-level breakdown for Japanese?
[08:36] Maya: yes, will include. often we see differences in tokenization that impact latency especially with CJK scripts.
[08:44] Samir: one more on model list — please also include an LLM with instruction tuning specifically trained on technical docs if available (a domain-focused smaller model).
[08:54] Maya: we will look for smaller domain-adapted checkpoints; if not available we'll run LoRA adapters on a 3-5 epoch quick train as a comparison.
[09:04] Ethan: recap — action items and dates as discussed, we will send pricing and benchmark template. Next meeting: kickoff week of 2027-11-15, we'll plan a 60-minute engineering sync.
[09:18] Anna: sounds good thanks.
[09:20] Ethan: thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
